question: According to the European Drug Report 20241, in 2022 some 6 400 people died in the EU from a drug overdose. Heroin alone was responsible for the deaths of 1 800 people. However, the biggest concerns relate to fentanyl, which, together with other synthetic opioids, could dominate these tragic statistics. In 2022, fentanyl overdose caused 163 deaths in the EU.

The biggest toll was in Germany (73), followed by the Baltic and Nordic countries2. These concerns are confirmed by preliminary data for 2023, including for my country. The surge in deaths and their geographical concentration, as well as conclusions from the United States, indicate that international criminal gangs are engaged in drug distribution in Europe.

This is confirmed by the fact that 14 EU countries reported seizing in 2022 more than 3 kg of nitazene, produced almost exclusively in China. In 2023, in relation to the situation in Syria, the EU imposed sanctions on individuals and entities responsible for the production and sale of Captagon3.

The US has taken a range of decisive action in recent years, imposing sanctions on Mexican smuggling cartels and Chinese fentanyl producers4 and raising the issue at the highest level in bilateral relations with Beijing5. The EU meanwhile has remained passive. 1.
Why has the Commission not taken measures similar to those concerning the smuggling of Captagon from Syria?
Following the US example, is the Commission planning to impose sanctions on entities responsible for producing and smuggling fentanyl and its derivatives and money laundering?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.1.2025) The Commission works closely with the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA) and Europol1 to monitor the situation of synthetic drugs across the EU, including captagon and fentanyl.

With its new mandate2, EUDA has strengthened its threat assessment capabilities and is developing a European drug alert system to facilitate the exchange of information on developments requiring rapid actions to safeguard health, social aspects, safety and security. The fight against drug trafficking is one of the priorities of the EU Drugs Strategy 2021-20253 and action plan4.

Penalties in the field of illicit drug trafficking are governed by Council Framework Decision 2004/757/JHA5. The Council Framework Decision 2008/841/JHA on the fight against organised crime6 foresees penalties for offences relating to participation in a criminal organisation. The Commission also adopted a dedicated EU roadmap7 envisioning exchanges with China.

The EU Drugs Dialogue was notably used to systematically raise the issue of drug precursors and synthetic drugs and ask China to take effective measures. There are also specific exchanges via the EU-China joint follow-up group meetings on drug precursors and on customs cooperation to help prevent the entry of designer precursors8 in the EU territory.

In April 2023, the EU decided to list 11 individuals and 3 entities in the framework of EU restrictive measures in view of the situation in Syria9 targeting those responsible for the production and trafficking of narcotics, notably captagon.

The trade in amphetamine has become a regime-led business model, providing its inner circle with revenue that contributes to its ability to maintain its policies of repression against the civilian population10.
